title: Better outcomes in babies with bacterial meningitis
official: Better Outcomes in Babies with Bacterial meningitis (BOBBi) – a multisite, open-label, two-arm, parallel-group, pragmatic, randomised controlled trial to compare dexamethasone versus no dexamethasone as treatment in babies with suspected or confirmed bacterial meningitis
summary:
Background and study aims
Meningitis is an infection around the brain and spinal cord. In babies under 3 months, even with antibiotics around 1 in 20 die and 1 in 3 survivors have lifelong disabilities. In older children, steroids given with antibiotics reduce some harm, but it is not known whether this also helps young babies. The aim of this study is to determine whether giving dexamethasone to babies with suspected or confirmed bacterial meningitis improves survival and reduces long-term problems.

Who can participate?
Babies up to 3 months of age who doctors think have bacterial meningitis.

What does the study involve?
Babies will be randomly allocated to receive dexamethasone or standard care shortly after starting antibiotics. Because bacterial meningitis is an emergency, babies may be enrolled into the trial before parents are approached, using a deferred consent model. Parents will usually be approached within 48 hours, provided with information about the study, and asked for consent for their baby’s ongoing participation and follow-up until 2 years of age.
Parents may withdraw their baby at any time without affecting their care. If a baby is later found not to have bacterial meningitis, study treatment will be stopped.
Parents will be asked to complete questionnaires at hospital discharge and at 12 and 24 months. Information from medical records will also be collected. Outcomes include survival and developmental difficulties such as deafness, reduced vision, seizures, cerebral palsy and learning problems.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
The trial addresses uncertainty about whether dexamethasone improves survival and long-term outcomes in babies with bacterial meningitis and may help improve future treatment.
As bacterial meningitis is an emergency, treatment must start quickly. Based on advice from parents with experience of bacterial meningitis in their baby, the trial uses deferred consent so that treatment is not delayed and parents are not overburdened during a critical situation. Parents are approached as soon as clinically appropriate by trained staff, usually within 48 hours, to discuss the study and provide written informed consent for ongoing participation.
Dexamethasone is commonly used in babies for inflammatory conditions and is recommended for older children with meningitis, although like all medicines it can cause side effects. Potential short-term risks include raised blood glucose and, rarely, gastrointestinal bleeding. Babies will be closely monitored throughout their care.
To minimise risks, very preterm babies (<34 weeks) are excluded from receiving dexamethasone during the first week of life, treatment is stopped if bacterial meningitis becomes unlikely, and all serious events are reviewed by the trial team and an independent data monitoring committee. Parents and charities helped design the study and continue to advise on the trial.

Where is the study run from?
The National Perinatal Epidemiology Unit Clinical Trials Unit (NPEU CTU) at the University of Oxford, England, UK, in partnership with City St George’s, University of London, sponsor for the UK sites, and the University of British Columbia, sponsor for the Canadian sites, are coordinating and managing the study.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The total planned trial period is 1 September 2025 to 31 August 2033, with recruitment planned from 1 June 2026 to 30 November 2030

Who is funding the study?
Health Technology Assessment Programme (UK) and Canadian Institutes of Health Research (Canada)

Who is the main contact?
Vasha Bari, bobbi@npeu.ox.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Babies must fulfil one of the following age-based criteria:
1.1. Babies born at ≥ 37+0 gestational weeks:
1.1.1. Up to and including 3 months from their birth date
OR
1.2. Babies born at 34+0 to 36+6 gestational weeks:
1.2.1. Up to and including 3 months corrected age
OR
1.3. Babies born less than 34+0 gestational weeks:
1.3.1. Are between 32+0 corrected gestational weeks and 3 months corrected age inclusive
AND
1.3.2. Are older than 7 days of age
2. Planned or initiated treatment with antibiotics for suspected or confirmed bacterial meningitis based on having one or more of the following three clinical and/or laboratory features: 
2.1. Seizures or bulging fontanelle or altered consciousness (coma)
2.2. Blood C-Reactive Protein (CRP) ≥20 mg/L* AND one or more of: 
2.2.1. Raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) white cell count (>20/mm3 for neonates ≤28 days post birth; >5/mm3 for babies >28 days post birth)** 
2.2.2. CSF protein ≥0.8 g/L**
2.2.3. CSF/blood glucose ratio <0.5 
3. Positive CSF Gram stain OR positive CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for a relevant bacterium OR CSF culture for a relevant bacterium

*If CRP is not available then an abnormal procalcitonin (PCT) threshold may be used instead (i.e., ≥0.5 mg/dL)
**When interpreting the results of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) investigations, take into account red cells in the sample, which may suggest blood contamination or a different diagnosis. In the case of blood contamination if the CSF RBC count is >=1000 cells/µL then CSF WBC and CSF protein should be adjusted
- subtract 1 WBC per 500 RBCs
- subtract 0.01 g/l protein per 1000 RBCs
Exclusion criteria:
1. Where the randomisation cannot occur within 12 hours of the first administration of antibiotics for meningitis, or within 12 hours of the first administration of changed dose/type of antibiotics where antibiotics have been changed in dose or type for newly suspected or confirmed meningitis
2. Previous neurosurgical intervention or shunt
3. Known hypersensitivity to dexamethasone or any of its excipients 
4. Previous randomisation into this trial
